Teaching

My teaching experience spans computer science introductions, high-performance computing and scientific computing. I strongly believe that good learning environments come from having a "just-hard-enough" challenge and an empowering classroom. You can read how I try to inculcate this environment in my teaching statement.

Teaching influences

A few writers and teachers have shaped how I think about teaching in CS.

  • From Edsger Dijkstra’s A Discipline of Programming, I take the idea that correctness—and, in my own work, performance—should be reasoned about through design rather than recovered after implementation.
  • Jeannette Wing’s “Computational Thinking” shaped how I think about computing as the broader skill of formulating problems so that humans and machines can participate in solving them.
  • From Elizabeth Zimmermann’s Knitting Without Tears, I take the importance of giving learners enough understanding to stop following recipes blindly and begin making informed choices of their own.
  • Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed gave me the idea of education as preparation to engage with a world that is “not as a static reality, but as a reality in process, in transformation.”
  • bell hooks’ Teaching to Transgress gave me language for the classrooms in which I have learned best: intellectually demanding, participatory spaces where learning is something the class does together.
